new_statements.quote: Stress tends to occur on the second last syllable of the word. In a four syllable word, however, there may be light stress on both the first and third syllables. There seems to be a change of stress when there is a change of intonation or focus. [...] The names of trees and birds tend to be stressed on the last syllable. [...] Word stress tends to be lost to phrase stress which is often accompanied by length and often falls on the last syllable of the word in focus.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and by default penultimate (confirmed by the SIL OPD 1992/96: 'Stress usually occurs on the second last syllable'); in four-syllable words light stresses fall on the 1st and 3rd (i.e. alternating, penult still prominent); a lexical class (tree and bird names) tends to final stress; some disyllables with a closed final syllable are transcribed with final stress (mbwi'yʌk 'rat'), matching Laycock's 1965 Wosera rule that a closed second syllable attracts stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Wearne & Wilson: four-syllable words may have light stress on both first and third syllables ('ʌkʰi'tʰəwe, 'mulʌs'kwiwu). Laycock 1965 (Wosera): secondary stress on any nucleus adjacent to the primary if of equal rank, and iteratively re-applied after an unstressed nucleus, so no more than three unstressed nuclei in a row.
new_statements.exceptions: Names of trees and birds tend to final stress (ma'sʌ 'betel nut', kwu'mun 'bird sp.'); closed final syllables can carry stress in disyllables; Laycock 1965 pp.29-30 instead analyses Wosera-dialect stress as weight/quality-sensitive within the first two syllables of the phonological phrase (higher-ranking nucleus wins; ties go to the first syllable in disyllables unless the second is closed, otherwise to the second syllable), with phrase-final open syllables never stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tendency stated on citation forms; both W&W and Laycock say word stress yields to phrase stress: W&W 'word stress tends to be lost to phrase stress... often falls on the last syllable of the word in focus' (nɨ'wʌ· lɨ ro 'mother she sits' vs 'nɨwʌ 'mother'); Laycock defines stress over the phonological phrase (one primary stress per pause-free stretch). W&W and Wilson describe the Maprik (northern, Samu-Kundi) dialect; Laycock the Wosera (Kamu-Kundi) dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: Wearne & Wilson 1970, the SIL OPD and Wilson 1980 describe the Maprik (northern, 'Samu-Kundi') dialect of Ambulas (data mainly from Yamikum village); Laycock 1965 describes the Wosera ('Kamu-Kundi') dialect recorded at Kunjingini, which Glottolog/Ethnologue keep inside Ambulas [abt] ambu1247 (distinct from Hanga Hundi/West Wosera [wos]). The two dialect descriptions give different formulations of the stress rule (penult tendency vs. nucleus-rank-sensitive within the first two syllables of the phrase).

sources.note: Sec. 5.3.1 (p.31): stress tends to fall on the second-last syllable of the word; four-syllable words may carry light stress on 1st and 3rd syllables; names of trees and birds tend to be stressed on the last syllable; word stress tends to be lost to phrase stress, which often falls (with length) on the last syllable of the word in focus. Examples with stress marks given.

sources.citation: Laycock, Donald C. 1965. The Ndu language family (Sepik District, New Guinea). Pacific Linguistics C-1. Canberra: Australian National University. Part II: Phonology and grammar of Abelam (Wosera dialect), sec. 5.2 Stress, pp.29-30.
sources.note: 'Stress is non-phonemic, being wholly conditioned by the syllable and nuclear structure of the phrase.' Primary stress falls on the higher-ranking nucleus (complex aw/ay > simple; a > ʌ > ə) of the first two nuclei of the phonological phrase; if equal in rank the first N is stressed unless the second syllable is closed or the phrase has more than two syllables, in which case the second N is stressed; a phrase-final open syllable is always unstressed; secondary stress on adjacent equal-rank N and iteratively after an unstressed N. Examples: /mə́nə/ 'you', /kə́pma/ 'ground' vs /vətɨ́k/ 'two', /…
